text: Technical debt -- when to pay it down versus ship around it. "We should really refactor this" is one of the most common sentences in engineering, and one of the least consistently followed up on, usually because nobody runs the actual numbers. This lesson treats technical debt as a real financial decision with a computable break-even point, not a vague feeling that something is messy.

Here's the debt. Northbeam's prompt-assembly logic -- how retrieved documents get formatted into the model's input -- has been copy-pasted into five different code paths as the product grew. Every time that logic needs to change, an engineer has to find and update all five copies, at roughly two extra hours of work compared to a single shared implementation. This happens about once a month.

Run the numbers. Two extra hours, twelve changes a year, at ninety dollars an hour fully loaded, is twenty-one hundred sixty dollars a year in carrying cost. Refactoring into one shared implementation is estimated at one engineer-week, thirty-six hundred dollars. Divide that by the monthly carrying cost and the break-even point is twenty months. This single number reframes the whole decision.

It's not "should we clean this up" in the abstract -- it's "do we expect this code to still be in active use, getting monthly changes, twenty months from now?" If the roadmap replaces this exact logic within a year, the refactor never breaks even -- you'd pay the cost and then retire the code before the savings show up. If it's expected to be stable for years, it's a clear win. That forward-looking question is exactly what a Staff or Principal engineer asks, and exactly what a mid-level engineer focused only on "this code is messy" often skips.

Sometimes the right call genuinely is to leave the debt in place and build around it -- not out of laziness, but because the break-even math doesn't support paying it down given the code's real expected lifetime, or because something more urgent has a better return on that same engineering time right now. "Ship around it" should be a deliberate, reasoned decision, ideally captured in an ADR, not a default that happens by never explicitly deciding anything.
Next up: roadmapping -- turning a business goal that says nothing technical at all into a sequenced technical plan.
